title: Neurobiological mechanisms of auditory training as a cognitive remediation strategy in schizophrenia probed by real‑time fMRI neurofeedback
summary:
Many people with schizophrenia have difficulties with attention, memory and learning. Research suggests that these problems are partly related to how the brain processes sounds and speech. Training programs with listening exercises on a computer or smartphone can help, but it is still unclear how they work in the brain and which brain areas are most important.

In this study, we aim to investigate which brain regions need to be engaged for auditory training to actually lead to improvements in attention, memory, and learning.  All participants complete several weeks of training with short tasks using tones and speech. In addition, several examinations are carried out in the clinic. These include brain scans, interviews, simple tests of memory and concentration, voice recordings, blood and breath samples, and an eye examination.

During some of the brain scans, participants receive a simple feedback display showing how active a certain brain region is and try to influence this activity by using different thoughts. We compare two versions of this training that focus on different brain regions. This should help us to better understand how the listening training works in the brain and how such programs can be improved in the future.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Persons can participate in the study if all of the following conditions are met:
They are at least 18 and at most 80 years old; they have a medically confirmed diagnosis of schizophrenia; they are able to understand the study information and to make an informed, voluntary decision about participation; and they are willing to sign the written informed consent and to attend several examination visits as well as the auditory training.
Exclusion criteria:
Participants will be excluded from the study if any of the following criteria apply: age below 18 years or above 80 years; lack of capacity to provide informed consent and absence of valid consent by a legally authorized representative; presence of a comorbid psychiatric or neurological disorder that is clinically predominant and would substantially interfere with the interpretation of study outcomes; contraindications to MRI (including metallic implants incompatible with MRI, pacemakers, cochlear implants, severe claustrophobia, extensive tattoos in the head or neck region or large‑area tattoos exceeding safety recommendations for MRI); pregnancy at the time of study participation; or individuals who are involuntarily detained in an institution on the basis of an administrative or judicial order or authorization.
